[[File:South Africa Headcount Index, First Tier Cities (5457977904).jpg|thumb|Head count ratio in [[South Africa]]]]
The '''head count ratio''' ('''HCR''') is the [[population proportion]] that exists, or lives, below the [[poverty threshold]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tendulkar|first1=Suresh D. |author-link1=Suresh Tendulkar|last2=Jain|first2=L. R. |title=Economic Reforms and Poverty |journal=[[Economic and Political Weekly]] |volume=30 |number=23 |date=June 10, 1995 |pages=1373–1375, 1377 |jstor=4402854}}</ref> One of the undesirable features of the head count ratio is that it ignores the depth of [[poverty]]; if the poor become poorer, the head count index does not change.<ref>{{cite book|last=Ravallion|first=Martin |author-link=Martin Ravallion|url=http://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/965061468739145705/pdf/multi-page.pdf|title=Issues in Measuring and Modeling Poverty|date=June 1996|series=Policy Research Working Paper|volume=1615 |place=Washington, D.C.|publisher=[[World Bank]] |access-date=2020-11-20}}</ref> For example, the poverty head count ratio at national poverty line (percentage of population) in [[India]] was last reported at 21.9% in 2011.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.NAHC?locations=IN|title=Poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population) - India |website=World Bank Open Data|access-date=2020-11-20}}</ref> In July 2012, ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported the poverty head count ratio as 11.1% of the population of the [[United States]] in 1973, 15.2% in 1983 and 11.3% in 2000.<ref>{{cite news|last=Edelman|first=Peter |author-link=Peter Edelman|url= https://www.nytimes.com/2012/07/29/opinion/sunday/why-cant-we-end-poverty-in-america.html |title=Poverty in America: Why Can't We End It?|date=July 28, 2012|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2020-11-20}}</ref>
